output:
Monsieur l'Inspecteur,

I have sat at this table since before the stove was lit, and I write because you will want the order of things, and because I would rather you had it from me than pieced it together from Rosa's kitchen clock.

You will have noticed that everyone in this town sets his watch by the Temple. Aurèle made a sermon of it every morning. I did the same for thirty years and never thought it a virtue or a fault. In La Chaux-de-Fonds time is something one agrees about, and I had agreed about it so long that I forgot it could be argued.

My watch was two minutes fast all evening. I told you I left the salon at a quarter to eleven by it. That was accurate in its own terms and false in every other. I knew the watch ran fast. Aurèle had told me so at dinner, as he tells everyone.

Jules died in 1889 of a dose I gave him. I raised it on a bad night because he was in pain and I was tired of being asked for more. I signed the certificate as the heart. No one in this town thought to ask a physician about his own arithmetic, and I did not offer it. For ten years it was a small, well-kept fact, like a watch in a drawer.

Aurèle found Jules's last letter among the papers he was sorting for the new century. He came to me in the hall before dinner, quite calmly, and said he would tell Félix at midnight and the authorities after. "At the turn of the century I settle my accounts." I do not think he meant it cruelly. There was simply no argument in him to be had.

I went up while Odile played for me. I will not describe the room. You have seen it. I struck him once. He fell and pressed the slide of the repeater he had spent four years on, and it sounded ten: two doubled notes, then eight high. I counted it. Anyone in this town would have counted it.

That is the minute I could not move. I could stop the regulator, and I did. I could set its hands back to five past ten, when I had been at cards with Odile in plain view, and I did that too. But a repeater cannot be made to unsay what it has said. I did not think of who might be listening in the street.

I came down, took the cigar case from my coat, and went back to the salon. Odile stopped playing when I came in. The hall clock struck its hour a moment later. It runs fast, as everything in that hall does, and I had long ago stopped hearing it.

*Primum non nocere.* I taught that to students for many years and was never troubled by its Latin. I am troubled by its grammar now.

I have asked Rosa to see that Odile has her breakfast. I shall be at the police post when you come, and I shall not need to be fetched.

Casimir Vauthier
